result.title: Large language models for literature screening in pharmacovigilance: an evaluation against human reviewers.
result.authorString: Rivera A, Okafor B, Lindqvist C.
result.abstractText:
Background

Weekly literature monitoring for adverse drug reactions is labour-intensive.

Objective

We aimed to evaluate whether a large language model could screen medical literature for individual case safety reports.

Methods

We used 4,200 abstracts screened by two human reviewers at a marketing authorisation holder. The model was prompted with the screening criteria and compared with the human decisions.

Results

The model reached a recall of 97.1% and precision of 61.3% for valid cases, compared with the reference standard. Screening time fell by 48%.

Limitations

The study used a single company dataset and English-language abstracts only.

Conclusions

These findings suggest the model could support, but not replace, human literature screening.

result.title: Detecting duplicate individual case safety reports with record linkage and machine learning
result.abstractText: Duplicate reports distort safety signal detection in spontaneous reporting databases. We developed a machine learning classifier that combines record linkage features from case reports. Using 12,000 report pairs annotated by safety physicians, the classifier achieved an F1 score of 0.91. In conclusion, automated duplicate detection could reduce manual review.

result.title: Detecting duplicate individual case safety reports with record linkage and machine learning.
result.abstractText: Duplicate reports distort safety signal detection in spontaneous reporting databases. We developed a machine learning classifier that combines record linkage features from case reports. Using 12,000 report pairs annotated by safety physicians, the classifier achieved an F1 score of 0.91 on an independent validation dataset from a second national database. A limitation is that only English narratives were included. In conclusion, automated duplicate detection could reduce manual review.

result.title: A deep learning model for causality assessment of adverse drug reactions
result.abstractText: Causality assessment of adverse drug reactions is subjective. We propose a deep learning framework that scores causality from case narratives.

result.title: Machine learning for hospital bed occupancy forecasting
result.abstractText: We trained gradient boosting models to forecast bed occupancy. Accuracy was 88%.

result.title: Artificial intelligence in signal detection: a scoping review

journal.title: Frontiers in Drug Safety and Regulation

result.abstractText: BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence is increasingly applied to signal detection in pharmacovigilance. METHODS: We searched four databases for studies published 2015-2025. RESULTS: We included 64 studies; most used disproportionality analysis with machine learning on FAERS. Few studies reported external validation. CONCLUSIONS: Evidence of operational use remains limited.
